name: Ahmadiyya
info: The Ahmadiyya Muslim Jama'at is an Islamic messianic movement that began in British India in 1889 under Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, who said he was the promised Messiah and Mahdi, and is known for its caliphate and its missions.

facts.origin: British India, formally on 23 March 1889, when Mirza Ghulam Ahmad took the oath of allegiance from a number of his companions at a home in Ludhiana; the movement took the name Ahmadiyya in 1900.
facts.founder: Mirza Ghulam Ahmad (1835–1908) of Qadian, who said he had been divinely appointed as the promised Messiah and Mahdi; since his death the Community has been led by a succession of Caliphs.
facts.scriptures: The Quran, with the sunnah and the ahadith, including the Kutub al-Sittah; the writings and recorded sayings of Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, and the collected record of his dreams, visions and revelations, hold a place in the Community's own literature.
facts.followers: The community gives a figure of "tens of millions"; independent sources estimate between 10 and 20 million worldwide, and other estimates run from 15 to 20 million. It was established in 209 countries and territories by 2016.

t: Ahmadis hold that Mirza Ghulam Ahmad was the promised Messiah and Mahdi, a prophet wholly subordinate to Muhammad, and that Islam is the final dispensation, to be restored to its original form and spread by peaceful means.

The Community is led by a Caliph, chosen by an electoral college, and its missions began abroad as early as 1913; it is described as the first Muslim missionary organisation to reach Britain and other Western countries.
Many other Muslims regard the recognition of Ahmad as a prophet as heretical. Pakistan has declared Ahmadis non-Muslims, and the Community says it has faced persecution and discrimination since 1889.
dyk: Ahmadis believe that Jesus survived the cross and died in Kashmir of old age while seeking the Lost Tribes of Israel, a view that departs from the mainstream Muslim belief.
ev: Mirza Ghulam Ahmad takes the oath of allegiance from companions at a home in Ludhiana, founding the Community
In a manifesto dated 4 November, Ahmad announces that the movement will be named for Muhammad's alternative name Ahmad
Ahmad dies and Hakeem Noor-ud-Din is elected the first Caliph
The first organised overseas mission opens in Putney, London
Mirza Basheer-ud-Din Mahmood Ahmad is elected the second Caliph, and a faction opposed to him forms the Lahore Ahmadiyya Movement
The second Caliph founds the city of Rabwah in Pakistan after the partition of India
The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation declares that the Ahmadiyya is not linked to Islam
After Pakistan issues Ordinance XX, the fourth Caliph relocates to London

sections.origins:
The Ahmadiyya is an Islamic messianic movement that arose in British India in the late 19th century. Its founder, Mirza Ghulam Ahmad (1835–1908) of Qadian, said he had been divinely appointed as both the promised Messiah and the Mahdi whom Muslims expect towards the end times, to bring about by peaceful means the final triumph of Islam. At the end of the 19th century he proclaimed himself the Centennial Reformer of Islam (Mujaddid) and gained a considerable following, especially in the United Provinces, the Punjab and Sindh. He and his followers believe that Muhammad and many other scriptures foretold his coming.

Formally, the Community's history begins on 23 March 1889, when Ahmad took the oath of allegiance from a number of companions at a home in Ludhiana. The movement emerged within Islam and also in response to the Christian and Arya Samaj missionary activity that was widespread in the 19th century. Ahmadis trace its history further back, to the early life of Ahmad, who reportedly began receiving revelations about his future, and to the traditions of various world religions.

The name came about a decade after the founding. In a manifesto dated 4 November 1900, Ahmad chose it with reference to Muhammad's alternative name Ahmad, and deemed it a blameworthy innovation to name an Islamic school after anyone but Muhammad.
sections.beliefs:
Ahmadis hold that the six articles of faith and the Five Pillars of Islam are the basis of their belief and practice, identical to those of Sunni Muslims. They accept the Quran as their holy text, face the Kaaba in prayer, follow the sunnah and accept the authority of the ahadith and of the four Rightly Guided caliphs. In jurisprudence they reject strict adherence to any one school, giving first place to the Quran and sunnah, though they usually base rulings on the Hanafi method where these sources are not clear. They believe in the absolute unity of God, and that all major world religions have divine origins and form part of a plan towards Islam as the final religion.

Several teachings are distinct. Ahmadis understand Khatam an-Nabiyyin differently from most Muslims: they hold that Muhammad was the last law-bearing prophet, but that new prophets wholly subordinate to him may still come. They regard Mirza Ghulam Ahmad as the Mahdi and the promised Messiah. They believe that Jesus survived the crucifixion and died in Kashmir, that no verse of the Quran abrogates another, and that hell is a temporary abode in which souls are cleansed.

Ahmadis divide jihad into three kinds: the struggle against the self, the peaceful propagation of Islam, and armed struggle, permitted only in self-defence against extreme persecution and then only on the Caliph's instruction. They also hold that religion and science cannot conflict.
sections.texts:
The Quran is the holy text of the Ahmadiyya, and Ahmadis accept the sunnah and the authority of the ahadith, using the Kutub al-Sittah, the six canonical hadith collections. They hold that the Quran is the final divine scripture and that its teachings are timeless; with the exception of the Quran, they believe the earlier scriptures are open to human interpolation. According to Ahmadi teaching, books outside the Abrahamic tradition, such as the Vedas and the Avesta, are also of divine origin.

The writings of Mirza Ghulam Ahmad hold a central place in the Community. The third Caliph oversaw the compilation of his dialogues and sayings, and directed the complete collection of his dreams, visions and verbal revelations. In one passage he gives his summary of the faith: to love God and to love humankind so much that one counts the suffering of others as one's own.

Later Caliphs added to this literature. The second Caliph, Mirza Basheer-ud-Din Mahmood Ahmad, wrote a ten-volume commentary on the Quran, and the Tehrik-e-Jadid scheme he launched produced a large body of writing in defence of Islam and of Ahmadiyya beliefs. The fourth Caliph wrote many books, among them Murder in the name of Allah and Revelation, Rationality, Knowledge and Truth. Under the first Caliph the Community oversaw an English translation of the Quran, and it has since translated the Quran into over 70 languages.
sections.spread:
The movement drew its first followers in the United Provinces, the Punjab and Sindh. Overseas missions began on an organised level as early as 1913, with the mission at Putney, London, and for many nations the Ahmadiyya was the first contact with preachers from the Muslim world. According to Richard Brent Turner, until the mid-1950s it was arguably the most influential community in African-American Islam.

Under the second Caliph, whose term lasted from 1914 to 1965, missions were established in 46 countries, mosques were built abroad and the Quran was published in several major languages. His Tehrik-e-Jadid scheme financed the training and dispatch of missionaries outside the Indian subcontinent. The third Caliph, Mirza Nasir Ahmad, extended the work, particularly in Africa: after a tour of West Africa in 1970 he set up the Nusrat Jehan Scheme, which now runs many medical facilities and schools there. In the post-colonial era the Community is credited with much of the spread of Islam in Africa.

By 2016 the Community had been established in 209 countries and territories, with concentrations in South Asia, West Africa, East Africa and Indonesia. It is a minority Muslim group in almost every country. In 2001 the World Christian Encyclopedia estimated that it was the fastest growing group within Islam.
sections.community:
The Community is led by a Caliph, whom Ahmadis regard as the resumption of the Rightly Guided Caliphate. They hold that a caliph is designated primarily by God, who guides the electors through visions, dreams and spiritual guidance; no campaigning is permitted. The office is above all spiritual, and the Caliph is also called Amir al-Mu'minin, Leader of the Faithful. The Majlis-ash-Shura, the Consultative Council founded in 1922, advises him, but he need not accept its views. The current and fifth Caliph is Mirza Masroor Ahmad, elected in 2003.

The Community is organised into national, regional and local communities, each with a president, called Amir at the national level. Five auxiliary organisations train members by age and sex, the largest being the Lajna Ima'illah for women over 15. Jamia al-Ahmadiyya, founded in 1906, trains missionaries, and the Jalsa Salana, an annual convention, is the most important function.

After the partition of India the second Caliph founded the city of Rabwah, in Pakistan, on 20 September 1948. The Community regards Qadian as its spiritual headquarters. The fourth Caliph moved to the Fazl Mosque in London in 1984, and the fifth moved the headquarters to Islamabad, Tilford, England, in 2019. Dissent over the nature of Ahmad's prophethood and his succession led in 1914 to the Lahore Ahmadiyya Movement, which has claimed 30,000 adherents.
sections.legacy:
Mainstream Muslims, who believe that Muhammad was the final prophet, have characterised the recognition of Ahmad as a prophet as heretical, and some regard Ahmadis as infidels. The Community says it has been subject to persecution and discrimination since 1889. In 1973 the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation declared that the Ahmadiyya was not linked to Islam, and in Pakistan the government has declared Ahmadis non-Muslims. Some Sunni Muslims use the terms Qadiyani and Mirzai for Ahmadis, which are names given by others that the Community never uses of itself.

In 1984 Pakistan promulgated Ordinance XX, which jeopardised the safety of the Community and made it impossible for the fourth Caliph to perform his duties, and he moved to London. Pakistan officially claims 290,000 Ahmadis, while Pakistani Ahmadis have boycotted the census since 1974; independent estimates run from 2 million to 5 million.

The Community has built over 15,000 mosques, over 500 schools and over 30 hospitals through its missionary council. It launched Muslim Television Ahmadiyya, the first Muslim satellite television network, and the charity Humanity First. Its motto, coined by the third Caliph, is love for all, hatred for none. Abdus Salam, a Nobel laureate and devout Ahmadi, is among its members.

summary: The Ahmadiyya Muslim Jama'at began in British India in 1889 under Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, whom its members hold to be the promised Messiah and Mahdi. Led by a Caliph and active in missions worldwide, it is regarded by many Muslims as outside Islam, and in Pakistan it has been declared non-Muslim by law.
references: Humphrey J Fisher, Ahmadiyya: a study in contemporary Islam on the West African coast (Oxford University Press, 1963)
notes: Source is the Ahmadiyya article only. Its Persecution section is two sentences, so the profile gives only what they say: persecution since 1889, the 1973 OIC declaration and Pakistan's declaration of Ahmadis as non-Muslims, plus Ordinance XX (1984) from the Fourth Caliphate section. No dates for the Pakistani constitutional amendment are given in the article; the third Caliph's section mentions it without a year, so none is stated.
Followers: the article gives 15 to 20 million in its lede and 10 to 20 million for independent sources, plus the community's own 'tens of millions'; all three are reported.
Dispute over standing: the article gives the mainstream Muslim view (heretical, Muhammad final prophet) and the Ahmadi view (Khatam an-Nabiyyin read differently); no verdict.
Written 'Hakeem Noor-ud-Din' and 'Mirza Basheer-ud-Din Mahmood Ahmad' as the article spells them. 'Ahmad' alone in section 5 on the second caliph is not used.
The article says the second Caliph's caliphate lasted 1914–1965 and that missions were set up in 46 countries 'during his time'; used as given.
The article says Mirza Ghulam Ahmad established the Community on 23 March 1889; start 1889, circa false.

Faith map: Indonesia and East Africa start in 2016 only because the article states concentrations there in 2016; earlier years are not supported. West Africa starts 1970 (the third Caliph's tour). The 1984 route runs from Rabwah to London, though the article says only that he left Pakistan; the Rabwah origin is my inference from its description as the city coordinating the Community's activity, and the editor may wish to move the point to a general Pakistan location.
Lahore Ahmadiyya claim of 30,000 is the article's 'unofficial' figure.
